slides.heading: Pythagoras' theorem: a² + b² = c²
bullets: How to find the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle by squaring the short sides, adding the squares, and taking the square root
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we build Pythagoras' theorem from squares on the sides of a 3-4-5 triangle, see exactly why the hypotenuse is 5 and not 7, and finish by untangling a tangent mix-up.

slides.heading: What we will learn
bullets: Find the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle using a² + b² = c²
Find a short side when the hypotenuse is known, and use the converse to test for a right angle
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

slides.heading: The triangle with short sides 3 and 4
bullets: A right-angled triangle has short sides 3 and 4 - what is the longest side?
Is it 7, because 3 + 4 = 7 - or something else?
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands and take two or three guesses without judging them yet; say: hold on to your idea, because the squares on the sides are about to settle it.

slides.heading: The squares add, not the lengths
bullets: Pythagoras' theorem: in a right-angled triangle, a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse
Square each short side first, add the squares, then take the square root to get the hypotenuse
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: the theorem is about the squares built on the sides, never about adding the side lengths themselves.

slides.heading: A right-angled triangle
bullets: The short sides are the legs a = 3 and b = 4, meeting at the right-angle marker
The hypotenuse c is the longest side, opposite the right angle, and it is still unknown
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the two legs draw themselves, the hypotenuse join them, and the small square marker appear in the corner for the right angle.

slides.heading: Squares on the short sides
bullets: The square on side a is 3 by 3: 3² = 9
The square on side b is 4 by 4: 4² = 16
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: a square grows on each short side and fills with unit squares - nine in the a-square, sixteen in the b-square. Keep the two counts, 9 and 16, in mind.

slides.heading: The square on the hypotenuse
bullets: The tilted square on the hypotenuse is filled exactly by the 9 unit squares and the 16 unit squares together
So the square on c holds 9 + 16 = 25 unit squares: c² = 25
slides.notes: Follow the dots as they fly into the tilted c-square: every one of the 25 slots is filled, nine blue and sixteen orange, with none left over - the two short-side squares exactly make the hypotenuse square.

bullets: The trap: c = 3 + 4 = 7, adding the lengths - but the bar of length 7 is too long
The truth: c = 5, because the squares add: 9 + 16 = 25 and the square root of 25 is 5
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: lengths add to 7, but the theorem adds squares. Watch the red trap bar shrink away and the green bar of length 5 match the hypotenuse.

slides.heading: Worked example: squares first, root last
bullets: Square the legs: 3² = 9 and 4² = 16, then add: 9 + 16 = 25, so c² = 25
Take the square root: c = 5 - never c = 3 + 4 = 7
slides.notes: Work this example line by line and keep the order strict: square, add, root. Ask the class to say the next step before you reveal it.

slides.heading: Practice: find the hypotenuse, and do not flip tangent
bullets: Find the hypotenuse for legs 6 and 8, and for legs 5 and 12, squaring before you add
Watch out for the flipped-tangent claim: tan = adjacent / opposite.
slides.notes: Work in pairs and check each other's order of steps. If a tangent appears, test it against the claim tan = adjacent / opposite. - that is the flipped version, and TOA says the opposite side goes on top.

slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove you can spot both traps
bullets: Find c for the 3-4 triangle and explain why c is not 7
Correct this claim before you leave: tan = adjacent / opposite.
slides.notes: On your own, no talking. The ticket checks the Pythagoras trap (c = 3 + 4 = 7) and the tangent trap in one place: tan = adjacent / opposite. is flipped - tan is opposite over adjacent.
